en: Preface to the Re-engraved *Record of Realization*:

The decline of the Great Dharma arises because our own school’s fundamental principles are not clearly understood; consequently, the patriarchal commands are not implemented, and demonic outsiders proliferate.
Even those as young as three feet tall plunder the leftover phrases of the ancient worthies, failing to distinguish between what is good and what is evil, and recklessly claiming them as their own.
How lamentable that usurpation is practiced so openly! The Song dynasty Chan Master Juefan was thus filled with apprehension.

He therefore combined and separated the teachings of the various schools, cited precedents for comparison, and adjudicated the essential tenets of the Five Houses. He went so far as to reveal their secrets and disregard what they held in taboo, not sparing himself of such acts.
Those of former times compared his intent to that of Guan Gao, Cheng Ying, and Gongsun Chujiu.
Alas! This is truly lamentable. This book is titled *Zhizheng* (Realization through Wisdom). Without wisdom, one is insufficient to discern the heterodox from the orthodox;
without realization, one is insufficient to administer rewards and punishments. Only when both illumination and function are complete can one truly shoulder the Great Dharma.

If one could fulfill the heart of Juefan, there would be such a person in the world who could read this book, directly investigate its fundamental principles, and carry out the ancestral commands. Thus it is said: [text continues].

It does not belie the intent of his writing. Even if one has not yet fully mastered this book, if they can propagate its transmission throughout the world to await that one person who might master it thoroughly, then even if they cannot immediately fulfill Juefan’s ambition, they are still one with whom Juefan would associate.
Among the works composed by Juefan are the *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha), the *Linjian lu* (Record from Between the Groves), and this [work].

The *Shuxiang* (Book of Calligraphic Characteristics) and its commentary have already been well-carved [into woodblocks]. Now, Yu Zhongfu of the Ministry of Revenue has again donated his own funds to carve this work.
That these three collections may circulate together in the world is indeed a source of joy for the Dharma-gate.
I hope that those who are dedicated to the Chan school will cherish and disseminate them; this is my earnest wish.
Recorded by the monk Zhìkě on the first day after the full moon in the sixth month of summer, the year Wànlì Yǐyǒu (1605), during the Ming Dynasty.

An Appendix to a Letter from Master Dáguān. Regarding the meaning of "realization through wisdom" (*zhìzhèng*): some interpret it as Vimalakīrti receiving various tactile sensations, as explained in the *Zhìzhèng* [commentary].
This, however, is not the intent behind Elder Hóng’s composition of this book. I have investigated this for a long time; you should understand it according to my own interpretation.

Take this as the standard. Master Zang, do not harbor any doubts regarding it. As for my preface, which is both unrefined and clumsy, you should take care to polish it together with Master Jiqu (Ji Kang). Only then may it be included in the carving.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Suppose there is a person who coats a great drum with a mixture of poisons and strikes it in the midst of a great multitude."
When struck, it emits a sound; even those who have no intention to hear it will all die upon hearing it, with the sole exception of one person who does not die an untimely death.
In this same way, the Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise:
wherever it is among the multitudes of various practices, those who hear its sound will find that all their greed, hatred, and delusion are completely extinguished. Although within them...

There are those who, even without conscious thought, are able to extinguish afflictions and have their various fetters spontaneously cease through the power of the causal conditions of this Great Nirvāṇa.

Even those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five heinous crimes, upon hearing this sutra, will likewise create the causal conditions for unsurpassed bodhi and gradually sever their afflictions—excepting only the icchantikas who meet with untimely deaths. It is further asked: what is meant by "secret"?
The secret treasury is like the letter *ī*. If the three dots were aligned side by side, they would not form the *ī*; if they were stacked vertically, they likewise would not form it.
Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara do they constitute the *ī* with its three dots.
If they were separate, they could not form it either. I am also like this: the dharma of liberation is not *nirvāṇa*, nor is the body of the Tathāgata *nirvāṇa*.
Nirvāṇa. Great Prajñā is also not Nirvāṇa. These three dharmas are distinct from one another, yet they are not Nirvāṇa.
I now abide within these three dharmas; for the sake of sentient beings, this is called "entering Nirvāṇa," like the worldly letter *i*.
The Transmission of the Lamp records that Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo once said: "The three sections of meaning in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are somewhat similar to the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen).
Now, to say they are 'similar' makes it clear that they are not the essential point of the School of the Patriarchs.
Nevertheless, although the essential point of the School of the Patriarchs cannot be seen within words and language, how could it ever be seen apart from words and language?"—Linji.
It is said: "In general, when raising the cry [of the Way], one must possess the Three Mysteries within a single phrase, and the Three Essentials within each Mystery.
To have both Mystery and Essentiality is the sound of the 'poison-dust drum. Two hundred years after Linji’s passing, there were still those who died upon hearing it.
Now, distinguishing guest and host is like the simultaneous existence of illumination and function; establishing lord and minister is like following from compassion."

Ming said: "A single phrase distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function operate simultaneously. If you can comprehend the meaning within this, it will be like striking the third watch at midday.
Tong'an said: "When guest and host are in harmony, it is entirely delusion; where ruler and subject coincide, the center itself is deviant.
How shall one sing the tune of returning home? Before the Hall of Bright Moon, the withered tree blooms. These words were as stated above.
None of these are encompassed by the teachings of a single lifetime. The third eye protruding from the face of Maheśvara is not an ordinary eye.
The *Pò sè xīn lùn* (Treatise on the Refutation of Form and Mind) states: "In the presence of form, the eye sees form; in other instances where there is no form, it does not see form."
This interpretation is incorrect. Why? Because within that dream, one perceives form where there is no form, and fails to perceive form where form exists.
The tradition states: "Regarding those in the realm of form, this refers to the time of waking; yet one does not see them during dreams.
Since there is no realm of form within a dream, to perceive forms therein is an inversion. This was the case with Liu Tian of Qi’s younger sister, the Princess of Wuyang.
The King was executed by Emperor Ming. The Consort, mourning him deeply, fell ill; no physician could cure her.

Zhen was skilled at painting women, while Yin Qian of Chen County was skilled at painting human faces. Zhen painted the King’s favorite consort, while he commissioned Qian to paint the King himself, both depicted as looking into a mirror together.
When the Consort saw them, she spat and cursed, saying, "It is only fitting that he should die young. Thereupon—
When affectionate attachment ceases, illness is swiftly eliminated; this is because when the heart of love ceases, inverted perceptions are extinguished.

The tradition says: The elder sister-in-law of Sun Yuzhi was widowed at the age of nineteen.

She vowed to eat but one meal for the rest of her life and recited the Lotus Sūtra, never marrying again. When Yuzhi was serving as the Magistrate of Gaoyang, his sister-in-law was already over seventy years old.

His countenance was radiant and his movements were light and agile. In the sixth month of summer in the sixth year of the Zhenghe era, he suddenly gathered his scriptures and arranged his clothing and ornaments for his handmaidens.
When they asked him the reason, he smiled and said, "I shall die in three days."
He passed away exactly as predicted. Han Zicang asked me, "When a person is about to die, there are those who possess foreknowledge.
What technique brings this about? I replied, "It is like cow's milk; when activated by a fermenting agent, although it occurs within the midst of causes and conditions..."
There is no agent; after a long time, it becomes curd. It does not come from outside, because it is produced within the milk.

Nor can it produce itself; it is brought forth by the addition of a fermenting agent (*maṇḍa*). Thus, through the ripening of conditions and causes, it is suddenly accomplished. There is a verse concerning this, which says in brief:
"Curd emerges from within the milk; there is no separate entity [other than the milk]. If one dies, why suffer? Why desire to know beforehand? It is like such-and-such a lady."
Taking a rest during the prime of life, one sees the results in white-haired old age. For more than fifty years, there has been no interruption in this constant mental application.

Spontaneously, one comes to know the days of transformation beforehand—just as curd is produced from within milk. Yet, observing the verses of Guifeng, I fear that [this realization] will occur at the time of death.

For example, when the Great Emperor Taizu of our own dynasty was about to launch a punitive expedition against the Southland (Jiangnan), the Ruler of Jiangnan dispatched his minister Xu Xuan to enter the imperial presence for interviews and recitations, intending to preserve his kingdom through his eloquence.
Upon meeting him, [the Emperor] said: "The Ruler of Jiangnan treats me like a father."
"His father serves Your Majesty; how can you wish to attack him? Taizu said, "Is it right for father and son to live apart?

Xuán was stunned and had no reply. That Xuán, who throughout his life knew by heart the verses of Guifeng, was nonetheless struck with such astonishment at the moment of death—this is precisely what happened here.
Chan Master Fengxue Zhao ascended the seat and said: "When the World-Honored One looked at Kāśyapa with his blue-lotus eyes—right at that moment, tell me, what did he say?
If you say he said nothing, then you will have buried the former sage. Before he had finished speaking—
Nian Fahua descended immediately. An attendant stepped forward and asked, "Why did Nian Fahua leave without saying a word?
Fengxue said, "He understood. The next day, Nian and the senior monk Zhen went together to the abbot’s quarters.
Fengxue asked Zhen, "What is the Buddha’s 'not-speaking speech'? Zhen replied, "The magpie cries atop the tree. Fengxue said, "..."

The *Chuan* (Biographies) states that Chan Master Wude of Fenyang composed a "Song of the Single Character.
Its essentials are as follows: "The Buddhas have never preached the Dharma; Fenyang briefly proclaims a single character. It is neither paper, ink, nor literary composition;

it is not the silent ground of Vimalakīrti. It further says: "Venerable Kāśyapa attained realization through shared illumination; with a blink of an eye, he respectfully executed the True Decree. This is the true leakless [transmission].

This reveals the family tradition. Formerly, Huangbo once sent Linji to deliver a letter to Guishan. After he had departed, Guishan asked Yangshan, "Ji-zi, what will become of this man in the future? Yangshan replied, "The Dharma-way of Huangbo relies upon this person; in the future, it will spread widely throughout the regions of Wu and Yue. However, it will stop when it encounters a great wind. Guishan said, "How so? Yangshan replied, "He will eventually become a teacher to the Emperor. Guishan said, "If that is so, then the Dharma will surely flourish. Later, when Linji was about to pass away, he told his disciples, "I have been ill for some time now. You should each compose a verse to express your realization. When the verses were presented, he did not approve of them. Finally, Nanquan’s verse was brought forward, and Linji said, "This one is acceptable. He then called out to Nanquan, who responded. Linji said, "After I am gone, you must go to the region of Wu and Yue. Nanquan replied, "I am already old and weak; how could I travel there? Linji said, "Do not worry; I shall send someone to escort you. He then called out to his attendant, "Bring me paper and ink. Having written something on the back of the verse, he said, "Give this to Master Nanquan. Later, Nanquan received it and saw that Linji had written: "When you arrive at the mountain gate, you will see a monk coming from the south. Tell him: 'The old man of the mountain gate has a message for you. If he asks, 'What is the message? you should say: 'Tell the old man of the mountain gate that the messenger has returned. Nanquan subsequently went to the region of Wu and Yue, where he indeed encountered a monk coming from the south. He said to him, "The old man of the mountain gate has a message for you. The monk asked, "What is the message? Nanquan said, "Tell the old man of the mountain gate that the messenger has returned. The monk then asked, "Where is the old man of the mountain gate? Nanquan pointed to the west and said, "He is over there. At that moment, the monk suddenly realized his original nature and attained great enlightenment. The *Biographies* state: The śramaṇa Huixiao of the Northern Qi, weary of his native village, lived in seclusion at Lingyan Mountain for several decades.

There was a man named Xiao who had been appointed as the Magistrate of Ren Mountain. Coming from his native village, he reflected early on that he had been away from home for a long time and thought to inquire whether his relatives and old friends were still living.

He went to the county seat to pay his respects to the Magistrate, but the Magistrate happened to have guests and Xiao was not permitted to announce himself. After a long while, Xiao suddenly realized: "It is not that the Magistrate is being dismissive toward a guest;
rather, it is my own feelings of attachment and aversion. Why should I be in such a hurry to dwell upon my homeland? Thereupon, he took up his visiting card and departed.
He said, "Alas! A lapse of mindfulness! Suddenly regaining his awareness, he then departed.
The Great Master, the Third Patriarch, said: "A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth."
The Biography states: When the Great Zen Master Si of Mount Nanyue had attained his past supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), obstacles soon arose again;
his four limbs became weak and flaccid, and he was unable to walk. He thought to himself: "Illness arises from karma, and karma arises from the mind.

At the source of the mind, there is no arising; what form can external objects take? Illness, karma, and the body are all like clouds and shadows. Having contemplated in this way, he... [fell into a trance].
Perverted perceptions cease, while pliancy remains as before.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "In a dream one may say it is many years, yet upon awakening it is but a brief moment; thus, although the time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa."
The *Śāstra* says: "Worthy Leader, that which is here called a single *kṣaṇa* refers precisely to non-thought (*amanasikāra*).

The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "I teach the meaning of *kṣaṇa* as the non-arising of all phenomena; that which arises at the very first moment is simultaneously subject to cessation. This is not taught for the sake of the foolish."
Because that which flows and turns in a single *kṣaṇa* necessarily lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*).
If it were not non-arising, it would not flow and turn. Therefore, only those who accord with non-arising perceive the *kṣaṇa*.
When Chan Master Huangbo Hui first visited Shushan, he asked: "What is it like when one departs in a single *kṣaṇa*? He replied: "It fills and pervades empty space."
"How will you go? Huì said, "It fills the void; it is better not to go. Shūshān then remained silent.
Huì went out and saw the First Seat, who asked Huì, "The words you just used in response were truly extraordinary. Huì said, "..."
"It also seems like a mere coincidence. I pray you will explain this for me. The First Seat said, "In a single kṣaṇa, can there still be room for deliberation?
At these words, Huì realized the essential meaning. I composed a verse: "Pervading the void, it arrives without traveling;
Within a single kṣaṇa, how could deliberation be tolerated? See it directly and immediately, Without falling into the realm of conceptual thought."
If the eye-organ wavers, it is already not [the true state].

The *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) says: "Because the characteristics of sensory objects undergo moment-to-moment transformation, this is precisely birth and death; by contemplating these characteristics of sensory objects..."
When the characteristics of arising and ceasing are exhausted, emptiness is found to be without substantial reality;
this is precisely nirvana. The Transmission says: "To conceptually differentiate dharmas such as form and sound moment by moment is called 'transformation.

To contemplate that these dharmas such as form and sound arise and cease without source is liberation in the very place [of their occurrence]. First, one contemplates one's own eye, saying: "This eye is itself non-existent..."
If one is able to see one's own body, yet even that very body cannot be seen, how can one see other things?
Next, observe the object before you: if you see this as a tree, how can it be a tree? If you see it as not a tree, how can you see it as a tree?
Next, observe the three periods of time: if what is presently seen exists, then the past and the future should also exist.
If the past and the future were non-existent, then the present would also necessarily be non-existent.

rather, they have already planted them in the presence of immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of Buddhas."

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the great-winged bird (garuḍa) takes dragons as its food. First, it observes the great ocean for those dragons whose lives are about to end;
it then parts the sea with its two wings, seizes them, and eats them. Thus one should know that this [teaching] is to be faithfully accepted.
This Dharma cannot be realized by those whose faculties have not yet matured. Zen Master Shen Ding Yin once said:
"When the attendant of Niaoke saw him blow a wisp of cloth onto him, he immediately attained realization of this matter.

Were it not for the long accumulation of pure karma and the practice maintained through vast eons, how could one be thus? Zen Master Fenyang Shao also composed a verse, beginning: "The attendant at first..."
His heart yearned for superior conditions, so he took leave of his teacher, intending to go and study Chan meditation.

When Niaoke recognized that his spiritual capacity (*indriya*) was ripe, he blew on a blade of grass, and [Yunyan] attained peace of mind in that very moment. Both elderly men were senior disciples of Shishuang;

they surely spoke thus because they had accumulated pure karma and their capacities had matured. Indeed, their profound source originated from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and this cannot be denied.
In recent times, heterodox Chan practitioners have said: "How could there be such awakening? Those who transmit awakening by brandishing a 'blow-off-hair' sword are merely using expedient means.
This is what is called being blind oneself while wishing to abolish the vision of the world.

The *Poxinlun* (Treatise on the Refutation of Form and Mind) states: "Just as when a person dreams, though there was originally no woman, they see a woman and engage in sexual union with her, resulting in the emission of impurity;
so it is with sentient beings. Since beginningless time, they have falsely experienced external objects such as form, fragrance, taste, and touch—all of which are likewise thus:
they are established despite being non-existent in reality."

The Tradition says: Regarding that which is said to be "truly non-existent yet accomplished," it was as when there were three brothers who heard that the courtesan Āmrapālī of Vaiśālī, the courtesan Sumana of Śrāvastī, and the courtesan Utpalavarṇā of Rājagṛha all possessed exquisite beauty; they thought of them day and night without ceasing.
He then dreamed that he engaged in sexual union with her. Upon waking, he thought to himself: "That woman did not come, nor did I go, yet the act of lust was accomplished.
Because of this, he realized: "Are not all phenomena likewise so? Thereupon, he suddenly attained the realization of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*).
The Wei general Zhang Liao and the Tang general Wang Yanzhang both possessed great prestige and fame; at that time, they were minor... [text fragment ends].
The child cried incessantly. His mother called out the names of two people, and the child’s crying ceased.
Although the young child did not yet recognize Zhang or Wang, his crying stopped as soon as he heard their names. How could this be anything other than the mind?

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "When the Rishi Viśvāmitra took Sudhana by the hand, Sudhana immediately saw himself traveling to worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields."
He beheld those buddha-fields and their assemblies, as well as the various marks and signs of excellence and the manifold adornments of the Buddhas;
this continued even for as long as hundreds of thousands of billions of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas as numerous as the atoms within those buddha-fields.
Finally, when that rishi released Sudhana’s hand, the youth Sudhana immediately saw himself returned to his original location.
The *Biographies* state: "As soon as he took his hand, he immediately entered the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

He saw that self and others were not separated by even the tip of a hair, and that from beginning to end there was no shifting from the present moment. When he let go of the hand, he emerged from meditative absorption. Yongming said:

"Thus we know that without moving from the ground of one's original station, the body pervades the ten directions; and without departing from within a single thought-moment, one returns [to the source]."
Though kalpas as numerous as motes of dust pass, its original position remains unmoved; the lands near and far are distinct, yet not a single thought-moment has shifted.
The long and short durations of time remain vividly present. The World-Honored One used the lotus as a metaphor, yet none in the world understand it; I alone understand it.
When a lotus is about to open its flowers, the seed is already within the flower, and the stalk is already within the seed—this is the nature of causes.
There is the fruit; within the fruit there is the cause. The three periods of time are simultaneous. Its seeds are distributed and further gathered therein;
they continue without interruption, and the ten directions are not separated.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: Mañjuśrī asked again, "In the face of the fear of birth and death, upon what should a bodhisattva rely?
Vimalakīrti replied, "Within the fear of birth and death, a bodhisattva should rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits.
Mañjuśrī asked again, "If a bodhisattva wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits, where should they abide? He answered:
It is said: "A Bodhisattva who wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merit should abide in the liberation of all sentient beings.
The Commentary states: "The cultivation of the Bodhisattva’s mind does not merely benefit others; it is precisely the means by which one benefits oneself.
Therefore, the former sages regarded the propagation of the Dharma and the deliverance of living beings as urgent, thereby cultivating the power of the Tathāgata’s merit."—By Xiushe Upāsaka.
Yi himself claimed to have attained the "Pacifying Banner of the Bodhisattva. Because sentient beings have not yet escaped birth and death, the Bodhisattva does not seek peace for himself.
Although the Bodhisattva has realized that the nature of birth and death is empty, he still feels fear toward birth and death;
thus, he has not yet attained ultimate peace and freedom from sorrow. If he can enter into birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, he will master birth and death.

As for those who can teach and transform sentient beings, this is the practice of universal nirvāṇa; being without emergence and without submergence, it is only then called the "Banner of Peaceful Security Free from Sorrow.
The Second Patriarch asked Master Bodhidharma, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth..."
“Bring forth your mind and I shall settle it for you. He replied, “When I seek my mind, it is utterly unattainable. Bodhidharma said, “I have finished settling your mind for you.
Master Zhuan said: I have heard the words of Dongpo: “It is like a person with diseased eyes who seeks a physician and is given light.”
"Clear. The physician said, "I have only medicine for removing cataracts; I do not have medicine for bestowing clarity.
If such clarity could be bestowed, it would itself be a cataract. Dongpo may truly be called one whose nature accords with the Way.
Yongjia said: "A great man wields the sword of wisdom; its prajñā-point is like a vajra-flame.
It not only emptily crushes the minds of externalists, but has long since struck down the courage of the heavenly Māras."
The Biography states: "When I first read this text, I imagined that this man’s divine countenance was extraordinary and his majesty eclipsed ten thousand monks, such that he was stern and inviolable.
Yet upon seeing his surviving portrait, he sat dejectedly on a simple wooden bed, his *kāṣāya* robe draped in a casual manner like that of a youth—such as the Vinaya Master Xuán.
Only then did I realize that because his mental faculties were so sharp and keen, the words he uttered were like knives and saws, capable of decisive severance."
One cannot seek [the Buddha] by means of physical appearance. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"These twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same name, Sūryacandrapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp-Brightness). They also shared the same clan name, Bharadvāja.
Bharadvāja means 'sharp faculties' (*tīkṣṇendriya*), which is also called 'swift,' and also called 'full speech. Regarding all dharma-gates, because of their sharp faculties and swiftness..."
Only those who quickly and fully clarify their speech can transcend birth and death. Liu Xiao of the Liang dynasty served the Buddha with diligent devotion;
suddenly, an old man appeared without cause and said, "Your mental power is firm and fierce; you will surely break through birth and death.
When Liu Xiao passed away, there were indeed miraculous signs. Nowadays, practitioners merely call this "running after the Way," yet in reality, they are lazy.
Falling into delusion and intoxicated by dharmas such as form and sound, he was like a fly stuck in saliva;
yet, savoring the lifelong practice of Yongjia, he was like a fragrant elephant breaking its chains and reins to depart with sovereign ease—truly a bhikṣu indeed.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "A straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it is free from falsehood.
The Transmission says: "What is called the 'eye that discerns dharmas' is the hand extended by former sages. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
"If practitioners of the path cannot achieve unexcelled *bodhi*, they may instead become *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, or [attain other states]."
The non-Buddhists, the various devas, the Māras, and their retinues all fail to realize the two kinds of fundamental roots;
thus they practice in a confused manner, like one who wishes to prepare a fine meal by boiling sand—though they pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they will ultimately never succeed.
"What are these two kinds, Ānanda? The first is the root of birth and death from time without beginning;

it is that which you and all sentient beings now take as your own nature—the mind that clings to objects. The second is the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa from time without beginning;
it is that which is now your essential clarity of consciousness, capable of giving rise to all conditions, yet which is lost amidst those very conditions."
This is precisely the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*). The攀緣心 (*ālambana-citta*,攀緣心) is that which is false and provisional. Yongming said: "Mind (*citta*) means faith (*śraddhā*).

This refers to when there are preceding consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) that follow along with phenomena according to their characteristics; in such a case, it is called affliction (*kleśa*) and is termed "consciousness," not "mind. As for "intention" (*manas*)...
It is recollection. Recollecting and conceptualizing past objects gives rise to delusion; these are all deluded consciousnesses and have no concern with the mind.
The mind is neither existent nor non-existent, and it is not defiled by existence or non-existence. The mind is neither defiled nor pure, and it is not sullied by defilement or purity.

Even confusion and awakening, ordinary and sagehood, coming and going, and staying—all these are deluded consciousnesses and not the mind. The mind is fundamentally unarisen; now, it likewise has no cessation.
If one knows that one’s own mind is thus, then the Buddha is likewise so. Yet Changsha’s verse says: "The student of the Way does not recognize the Real;
it is only because they have long been identifying with the conscious spirit. Since time immemorial, this has been the root of birth and death, yet deluded people call it the 'original person'.
Nowadays, false Chan is being transmitted and taught, using such gestures as raising the eyebrows, blinking the eyes, or brandishing the whisk.

To take the raising of the mallet as the ultimate limit—how could the Buddha-dharma be so nearly submerged? The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "Sentient beings wander through deluded perceptions.
Those who weary of this wandering falsely perceive nirvāṇa; because of this, they cannot enter pure awakening.
It is not that awakening rejects those who seek to enter it; rather, there are those who seek to enter, yet it is not by means of their entering that awakening is reached. This refers to liberation.

There are those who are able to enter the path of awakening, yet they achieve only the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and are not able to enter true awakening; therefore it is said, "because it is not an entry into awakening.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was no dharma by which he attained Anuttarā..."
“Was there any dharma by which the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? “No, World-Honored One.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there was no dharma by which the Buddha, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Truly, there is no dharma by which a Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
"Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then the Buddha Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction:
'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Because, in reality, there is no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, therefore..."
The Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni.
Why is this? Because "Tathāgata" has the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.

Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi*, [they would be mistaken], for in truth there is no dharma by which a Buddha attains *anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, as for the Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata, therein there is neither reality nor unreality."
The Tradition says: "As for what is called 'that which the Tathāgata has attained,' within this there is neither reality nor emptiness.
This was the intention behind Bodhidharma’s coming from the East that he did not speak; yet in the world, few are able to know it, and even among those who know it, few are able to express it.
Sōngp’o said: “The Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet it is said that he attained it ‘by way of non-attainment.
Śāriputra attained the path of an arhat, and it is likewise said that he attained it ‘by way of non-attainment.
Are the Tathāgata and Śāriputra thus identical? He replied: ‘Not only Śāriputra; up to—’”

Among the various humble crafts of the artisan—catching cicadas with a willow twig, the "intention-hook" technique, treading on wild boars, and painting on a wall—there has never been one who did not achieve success.
When discussing the relative magnitude of the Way, even a Great Bodhisattva views the Tathāgata as being as far apart as heaven and an abyss.
Yet, when it comes to attaining through the principle of "non-attainment," then catching cicadas, the intention-hook, treading on wild boars, and painting on a wall are all one and the same.
There has never been anyone who was not identical to the Tathāgata. Dongpo’s words regarding my Dharma are like Du Mu’s discourse on military strategy, which says:
"It is like a pearl in a bowl; its rounding, turning, horizontal or diagonal movements cannot be known. All that can be known is that the pearl does not leave the bowl.
The Tathāgata manifests traces solely for the purpose of delivering sentient beings. If there were a dharma that could be transmitted, then...
He immediately conferred [the transmission]. However, as for the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), it clearly shows that there is no dharma that can be transmitted.

Zao Bo said: "In the third assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) were taught atop Mount Sumeru to symbolize entering the principle and acceding with wisdom, for this is not something that can be reached by a mind of arising and ceasing. Just as Mount Sumeru stands within the great ocean, it is eight..."

It is fourteen thousand yojanas [away], beyond the reach of hands or feet to grasp. This clarifies that the eighty-four thousand mountains of affliction (*kleśa*) abide within the great ocean of delusion.
When one is without thought or volitional action regarding all phenomena, the ocean of affliction is immediately dried up;

the mountains of affliction then become the mountain of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and the ocean of affliction becomes the ocean of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*). If one gives rise to mental deliberation, [the result is otherwise].
If there is anything upon which one relies, then the mountain of worldly toil becomes ever higher and the ocean of affliction ever deeper; thus, one cannot reach the summit of wisdom.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "You need only abandon birth and extinction, and maintain the true and eternal. Then the light of eternity will manifest."
At that moment, the sense organs, objects, and the perceiving mind all vanished instantly.

Therefore, the Great Being Vimalakīrti manifested his supernatural power, and immediately the Buddha Sumerudīparāja sent thirty-two thousand lion thrones—lofty, vast, magnificent, and pure—which entered the room of Vimalakīrti.
These were such as none of the bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings had ever seen before.
He saw that the room was vast and spacious, fully accommodating thirty-two thousand lion thrones without any obstruction.

Master Baojue said, "Given the height and breadth of the lion thrones and the narrowness of Vimalakīrti’s room, if one were to dwell upon this for even a moment, it would surely result in obstruction.
He once asked Xia Yi, the Commissioner of the Transport Office: "You say that... [the text here is incomplete].
"Inanimate things share one essence. At that time, there was a dog lying beneath the incense table. [Zhaozhou] then struck the incense table with a ruler and hit the dog, saying:
"The dog has sentience and thus departs; the incense table is insentient and thus remains.
How can they become one essence? The dog could not respond. Baoyue said: "As soon as one enters into deliberation, it becomes a superfluous dharma. The former sages..."
What is known has been transmitted from one to another; all of it is this very principle. Yet, scholars have been unable to clarify it.

For instance, it is said that by a mere snap of the fingers, five hundred venomous dragons were subdued, and even the meditative concentration of a woman emerged—this is particularly manifest and clear.
Guishan once said to Yangshan, "Ji-zi, speak quickly! Do not enter the realm of the aggregates," and so Yangshan...
Mount Shouyu said, "Huiji, even the stage of faith is not established. I regret that Yangshan’s ultimate power was not fully exhausted.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Ten Stages" chapter, says: "Birth and death both arise from the mind; if the mind is extinguished, birth and death are ended."
It is further said: "By conforming to ignorance, one gives rise to the various states of existence (*bhava*); by not conforming to them, existence is severed. The tradition says:
For example, it is like a person who fears his shadow and flees from the sunlight; the faster he walks, the more closely the shadow follows him.
If he rests in the shade of a tree, the shadow vanishes of its own accord. Even a child three feet tall knows this, yet scholars fear [the truth].
To ceaselessly extinguish the deluded mind within the cycle of birth and death is not analogous to this. It is like how when one draws close to a gentleman, the petty man naturally distances himself;
and when one draws close to a petty man, the gentleman naturally stays far away. This is something known even to commoners in the marketplace.
Yet those who study fear the suffering of saṃsāra and willingly comply with ignorance; they are like one who sets out from Shuoyue for Yan.
Now, once the mind’s quiescence is realized, habitual activities no longer arise;
when one does not unite with delusion, original wisdom naturally manifests before one. These two points concern only the mind; they require no further effort.
When the Third Patriarch, Chan Master Can, had entrusted the Great Dharma to the Fourth Patriarch, Chan Master Xin, he made this vow:
"Be careful never to say that you received the Dharma from me."
The *Zhuàn* says: The *Yì Jì* states, "The wills of the multitude do not go beyond the realm of food, drink, and sexual intercourse.
Generally speaking, regarding the resources for sustaining life, those whose resources are abundant have strong vital energy (*qì*), while those whose resources are meager have weak vital energy.
Therefore, when the vital energy (*qi*) overcomes the will (*zhi*), one becomes a mere physical soul (*po*). The worthy and sages are not so; they unify the will with the vital energy.

Thus, clarity and purity reside within their persons, and their will and energy are like the divine. Whether they are granted the lordship of the whole world or reduced to the state of a commoner, there is nothing that can diminish or augment them.

Therefore, when the will (*zhi*) overcomes the vital breath (*qi*), it becomes the soul (*hun*). When ordinary people die, they become ghosts; when sages and worthies die, they become spirits (*shen*).

This is not because they possess two different kinds of knowledge; rather, it is because the destination of their will differs. Judging the Three Patriarchs by this principle, I know that they were those whose will prevailed.
Master Song said: "This is likely because the Patriarchs took fame and traces as the Way."

Therefore, even regarding his own lineage of masters, he wished to sever it. One might then ask: does this not mean that what Master Can obtained through the Dharma was not truly the succession of the Patriarch?

This is most certainly not the case. At that time, Master Can reflected upon the difficulties faced by Bodhidharma and the Venerable Ke in propagating the Dharma, seeing how they were all slandered and harmed by heterodox teachers;
he merely took great pains to exercise caution for himself, and did not mean to say—
Is it permissible to abandon one's teacher?

Zen Master Huangbo Xiyun said: "When an ordinary person is about to die, they should simply contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty, the four elements are without self, and the true mind is without form—neither going nor coming.
When born, the nature does not come; when dying, the nature likewise does not depart."
Do not go. Remain profoundly still and perfectly quiescent; let mind and object be as one.

If you can thus achieve immediate and sudden realization, you will not be bound by the three periods of time and will be a person who has transcended the world. You must not have even the slightest inclination toward anything.
Even if you see auspicious signs such as the Buddhas coming to welcome you, or various phenomena manifesting before you, do not have the intention to follow them. If you see evil...
When various marks manifest before one, there is likewise no fear; rather, by simply forgetting the mind so that it becomes identical with the dharma-realm, one attains mastery.
This is the essential point.
The *Biographies* state that these were words spoken by Huangbo at one time for the sake of Prime Minister Pei. He was instructing him to forget the mind;

it need not necessarily be when approaching the end of life that one performs this contemplation. How do we know this? The *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* says: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts.
Regarding the various deluded minds, do not attempt to extinguish them. Abide within the realm of delusive thoughts..."
He added: "Regarding that which is known, there is no further knowing; because one does not discriminate regarding reality, the verse says:
'If sentient beings in the final age do not give rise to delusion in their minds, the Buddha says that such people are, in this very life, Bodhisattvas.
Guifeng categorized this as 'sudden realization through the forgetting of the mind. Observing the preceding meaning in light of this, I know it to be a provisional teaching."

I once examined the *Yun Gong Yishi* (Account of Master Yun’s Deeds). His original name was Xi-yun. During the calamity of the Huichang era, he covered his head with a white cloth and changed his name to Shen-yun.
When Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne, he restored the teachings and returned his name to Xi-yun.
This is something unknown within the monastic community.

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "The essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena are perceived by the world; how can one say they do not exist? It replies: "These are the false perceptions of the ignorant and should not be trusted.
Phenomena subject to arising and ceasing are entirely empty. Their arising and ceasing flow on in succession without a moment’s pause;
because they continue in a similar stream, the ignorant falsely perceive them as real, just like the flame of a lamp, which arises and ceases from moment to moment."
Ordinary, foolish people take this to be a single flame.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Just as a lamp, though it perishes moment by moment, yet possesses light that dispels darkness, so too are the dharmas such as mindfulness;
just as the food of sentient beings, though it perishes moment by moment, can nevertheless satisfy hunger."
One thereby attains full satisfaction. It is like a superior medicine: although it perishes moment by moment, it can nonetheless cure disease.
The light of the sun and moon, though perishing moment by moment, can nonetheless cause plants and trees to grow. Indeed, all phenomena perish and cease moment by moment;
yet they are perceived as presently existing because of their similar continuity. As the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* says: "Observe the dharmas with discernment..."
What is the nature of dharmas? Know that they are simply self-luminous; the dharmas themselves have no darkness. Both light and darkness are empty; there is neither action nor grasping.
If light were subject to action, it could not admit darkness; if darkness were graspable, it could not receive light.
Now, observe the darkness in a room at night: from where does it come? When a lamp-flame suddenly appears, where does the darkness go? —Shitou.
It is said: "Within light there is darkness" because light has no agency; "within darkness there is light" because darkness has no grasping.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"The World-Honored One, before the assembly of all beings, manifested great supernatural power and extended his broad and long tongue upward..."
Reaching the Brahma-world. A tradition says that Guishan once remarked: "When the sentiments of both the ordinary and the sage are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed;

when principle and phenomena are non-dual, this is the Buddha of Suchness. Yet students are unable to savor these words deeply; they merely rely on their own conjectures and estimations. It is like...

It is like a group of blind men feeling an elephant; each takes what they encounter to be the whole, so that the elephant is perceived only as a tail, a hoof, a waist, or a tusk, while the complete elephant remains hidden.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Without duality, without division, without distinction, and without interruption.
This refers to true permanence (*dhruva*). It is not a single, solid entity, nor is it a permanence that is fixed and immutable.
Yet those who interpret the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* say: "The Buddha’s voice is profound and subtle;

it is heard everywhere, transcending both ordinary beings and sages, for his tongue is broad and long, extending high above the Brahma world. Is this not almost a case of generating an interpretation based on mere words? It is erroneous!
The *Sūtra on the Fifty Calculations* states: A bodhisattva asked the Buddha, “When offenses arise and then cease, why is it that I do not perceive them?
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas, “Does your mind undergo transformation and birth? The bodhisattvas replied, “Our minds do undergo transformation and birth.
Even if our minds did not undergo transformation and birth, we would still be unable to converse with the Buddha. The Buddha then asked the bodhisattvas:
The Buddha said, "When a thought arises, can you still perceive that a thought has arisen? The bodhisattvas replied, 'We only recognize the presence of causes and conditions;
we do not perceive the initial moment of its arising. The Buddha said, 'If, as you say, you cannot even know when a thought first arises, how can you be free from fault?'"
The *Śāstra* says: "If it is said that the doubts of the various bodhisattvas constitute an offense, yet I alone do not perceive it, the World-Honored One replied:
'You are unable to know the initial arising of the mind; thus, while the offense exists, you do not see it. Yongming said:

"Therefore, we know that if one does not examine the provisional nature formed by the cause of the very first thought-moment, how can one avoid the fault of the subsequent thoughts continuing to form actualized events?"
Ah! By this I know that all birth-and-death and afflictions arise solely because of non-awakening.
If wisdom serves as the precursor, how could blame or fault arise? If one realizes that there is no phenomenon outside the mind, then emotional conceptions will not arise.
Without the need for further effort, one enters directly into the inconceivable stage.
The verse by Ānanda in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* says: "It has eliminated my inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas; without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, I have attained the Dharma-body.
The Commentary states: "I observe that in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, from the moment the various Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first surged forth, by means of..."
The Bodhisattvas praised the Buddha with various kinds of dharmic hymns.
Thus, fifty intermediate kalpas passed while Śākyamuni Buddha sat in silence, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for those fifty intermediate kalpas.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he caused the great multitude to perceive the time as being only half a day. Indeed, half a day—
During this interval, fifty minor kalpas pass, sustained by inverted perceptions.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* asks: "Based on faith, there are four kinds of discourse: first, direct perception; second, inference; third, analogy;"
4. Āgama. Among these various types of faith, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the most excellent.

If there were no external objects, how could people in the world say, "I am directly perceiving these things, such as blue or yellow"? The answer is given in verse: "Direct perception is like a dream;

that which sees and that which is seen do not coexist. At the time of seeing, there is no conceptualization. How, then, can one speak of 'direct perception'? For ordinary beings, it is a dream of afflictions."
Among these, whatever objects are perceived are all like those in a dream. Just as when one first sees a form, one does not know its meaning;

it is only later, through the discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), that one comes to understand it. This is because by the time the mental consciousness discriminates, the visual and other sensory consciousnesses have already ceased.
Because all phenomena do not abide for even a single moment: when one perceives form, the mental consciousness has not yet arisen;
and when the mental consciousness arises, the visual and other sensory consciousnesses have already ceased.
The *Zhuan* says: "For example, when people of the world look at the same text, those who do not know how to read see only the paper and ink, with no thought applied to the meaning or principle;
whereas those who know how to read see only the meaning and principle, without being hindered by the paper and ink.

Those who do not know how to read represent the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*); those who know how to read represent the sphere of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). — Tiantai.
The Master [Huiyuan] considered the five consciousnesses to be "regressive and residual," for this reason. Thus he said: "The seer and the seen do not coexist.

Now, paper, ink, and written characters exist for the purpose of transmitting principles and meanings; once these principles and meanings are grasped, what further use would there be for paper, ink, and written characters?

Regarding Caoshan’s “Food of Right Livelihood,” the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are three kinds of death: namely, death due to the exhaustion of lifespan, death due to the exhaustion of merit, and death due to not avoiding uneven conditions.
One should know that these are also deaths occurring at the proper time or at an improper time; or they may occur through a wholesome mind.
An unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind. What is death through the exhaustion of the life-span?
It is like a certain person who dies because the full measure of their allotted lifespan has been exhausted; this is called timely death. What is death due to the exhaustion of merit?

It is like a certain person who dies because of a deficiency in the necessities of life. What is death from not avoiding the uneven? As the Blessed One said, there are nine [types of untimely death]...
There are nine conditions by which one dies before the full span of one’s life has expired. What are these nine? They are: eating without moderation; eating at an improper time;

eating again before what was previously eaten has been digested; vomiting up what has been produced [as waste]; retaining what is undigested; failing to seek medical treatment; lacking knowledge of what is harmful or beneficial to oneself;
[eating] at the wrong time or in the wrong quantity; and engaging in unchaste conduct. These are called the [conditions of untimely death].
One dies at that time. Judging from this, I know that eating for the sake of eating is not a wrongful death; therefore, it is called "right livelihood" food. Huangbo said:
"Those who have only recently emerged [into the path] nowadays desire only to possess much knowledge and understanding, seeking extensively for textual meanings and calling this 'cultivation.
They do not realize that such abundant knowledge and understanding instead result in obstruction; they merely give more to their children."
Regarding ghee and milk, one knows nothing of whether they have been digested or not. Those who practice the path of the Three Vehicles are all like this;

they are all said to have "undigested food. This so-called "undigested food" refers to undigested intellectual understanding, which acts as a poisonous drug and is entirely categorized within the realm of arising and ceasing.
Since such things do not exist within True Suchness (Tathatā), by this we know that Caoshan values [the undigested].
Regarding the food of right livelihood, three types of falling away are established:
the falling away from not severing sound and form, the falling away that follows after them, and the falling away into nobility.
The tradition says: The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states, "One should accept food for the sake of destroying the mark of composite phenomena, and for the sake of non-acceptance."
One should accept that food with the perception of an empty village when entering a town. Regarding forms seen, one should be like one who is blind;

regarding sounds heard, like an echo; regarding odors smelled, like the wind; regarding tastes tasted, one should not engage in discrimination; regarding various tangibles felt, one should receive them as realized by wisdom;
and regarding all phenomena known, one should know them to be like illusions—devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of extrinsic nature, fundamentally non-existent from the beginning.
However, now there is no cessation; this is the basis for establishing that sound and form are not severed.
It is further said: "Subhūti, one does not see the Buddha, nor does one hear the Dharma.
