Chan Master Daowu Yuanzhe of Mount Gui said: "Practitioners of the Way must be careful not to allow their minds to be defiled.
Simply ensure that all manifold sufferings are exhausted, and that is the Buddha-mind."

The Transmission says: "That which is called 'the many sufferings' refers to the suffering of encountering the hated and disliked, the suffering of separation from the loved, the heavy suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the suffering of lacking resources for enjoyment, the suffering of wandering through sounds and forms, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of being harmed by other sentient beings."

Yet all these are merely matters of emotional attachment. Zao Bo said: "The essence of both ordinary beings and sages is true; it is only the barrier of views that remains. When views persist, one is an ordinary being;
when attachments are forgotten, one is a Buddha. These are truly ultimate words; even the former sages could not add so much as a hair’s breadth to them.
Yet those who have deep faith in this are rarely seen in the world. Such was Zen Master Zhidu of Lingyang Ruifeng. His...

He was indeed nearly equal to the sages. On the eighth day of the eighth month in the first year of the Kaibao era, he composed a verse, saying: "On the second day of the second month next year, I shall temporarily part from you.
My ashes and bones will be scattered across the Long River; Do not occupy the land of a donor.

On the twenty-eighth day of the first month of the following year, clergy and laity entered the mountain. He welcomed them with a serene smile, and all were greatly delighted. On an auspicious day in the second month, the local officials all assembled.
For several nights, the hall was as crowded as a marketplace. On the day of his departure, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly. The Elder Yuan Ying stepped forward and asked:
"The clouds grieve and the mists darken; what shall become of the great multitude? We pray you grant us a word before you must take your leave. As he spoke, Yuan Zhen lowered one leg from the seat.
Yuan Ying replied: "The Dharma-mirror does not descend upon this land; where else, then, will the Precious Moon shine? Yuan Zhen said: [He remained silent.]

"This is not within your realm. Duan said, "If that is so, then as bubbles arise and bubbles perish, they return to the water; the master departs and the master comes—this matter is fundamentally constant.
He then made a sound of sighing and asked the fourfold assembly, "At what time did the World-Honored One pass into parinirvāṇa?
The assembly replied, "On the fifteenth day of the second month at the hour of the rat (midnight). Duan said, "Today, at the hour of the horse (noon), I [shall do the same]. He spoke these words.
He passed away and was transformed.

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: The Bodhisattva Pure Karmic Obstructions asked, "If this awakened mind is pure by nature, for what reason is it defiled, causing all sentient beings to be deluded and distressed, unable to enter [it]? To which the World-Honored One replied only: "Sentient beings..."
Since beginningless time, one has falsely imagined and clung to the existence of a self, a person, sentient beings, and a life-span.

The *Zhuan* says: Zao Bo stated that, as the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana* says, "The aspect of inconceivable karma" means that, based upon the purity of wisdom, one is able to produce all supreme and wondrous realms—namely, the aspects of immeasurable merit—which are eternally non-existent.
It is severed. It manifests in various ways, spontaneously corresponding to the faculties of sentient beings, so that they may obtain benefit.
Furthermore, it is said: "Because awakening arises based upon original awakening (mūla-awakening). It is also said: "Based upon wisdom, suffering and pleasure arise."
As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* explains at length, all sentient beings are deluded regarding fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and thus there exist worldly suffering and pleasure.
Because wisdom has no inherent nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it fails to awaken according to conditions, and through the karma of suffering and pleasure, one becomes entangled by suffering.
Only when one attains self-awakening does one realize that the fundamental [wisdom] is without nature, that all conditions are without nature, and that the myriad dharmas [are likewise so].

Self-quiescence. When suffering is not perceived, because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one does not generally know whether there is intrinsic nature or the absence of intrinsic nature.
It is like a person who falls to the ground and rises from the ground. Question: All sentient beings inherently possess immovable wisdom (*akṣobhyajñāna*);
for what reason do they not spontaneously realize the true, eternal, and pure state? For what reason do they follow along with defilement (*saṃkleśa*)? Answer: All sentient beings... [text continues]
Because one gives rise to this wisdom, one is born within the three realms. This is because wisdom lacks inherent nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);

it cannot know for itself whether it is wisdom or non-wisdom, nor such phenomena as good or evil, suffering or pleasure. Since the essence of wisdom lacks inherent nature, it merely manifests according to conditions (*pratyaya*), like an echo in a valley that forms sound in response to objects.
Wisdom without inherent nature merely discriminates in accordance with conditions; through this discrimination, [it functions].
Therefore, delusion and craving arise accordingly. Because of delusion and craving, the sickness of "mine" arises.
Because there is "mine," the karmic activity of grasping at self and other arises. Because of this grasping, it is called *manas*. Because *manas* grasps, it is named "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Due to the seeds of consciousness, birth and death continue in succession. Because of birth and death, the various sufferings are immeasurable.
Because suffering is immeasurable, one seeks the path that is free from suffering. Those who are deluded and do not recognize suffering cannot give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Those who recognize suffering and seek the truth possess, in fact, original wisdom; it is precisely by encountering the conditions of suffering that one is able to know suffering.

Without encountering the conditions of suffering, one cannot know suffering. Because one knows the conditions of suffering, one is then able to give rise to the aspiration to seek the unsurpassed path.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: Furthermore, when sentient beings are about to die, until they reach the stage of the fainting of perception (*mūrcchā-saṃjñā*), the self-love (*ātmasneha*) practiced over a long period manifests before them.

By the power of this, thinking "I shall no longer exist," they then cherish their own bodies; it is by means of this that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and rebirth in the next life are established.
This is also the case for those who have attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) at that time.

Self-love (*ātmasneha*) likewise continues to manifest; however, these stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), through the power of wisdom, repeatedly investigate this self-love, restrain it, and do not adhere to it.
This is just as a strong man, when contending for strength with one who is weak and inferior, is able to subdue him.
You should know that the principle here is the same. As for the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) at that time...
"My love no longer manifests.
The tradition records that Master Guifeng said: "One should take emptiness and stillness as one's own self, and not identify with the physical body.
One should take spiritual awareness as one's own mind, and not follow deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all; then [the mind] will naturally..."
At the time of death, one abandons the short for the long and exchanges the coarse for the sublime.
If a practitioner can cause this contemplation to remain constantly manifest, it is truly the power of wisdom. At present, however, this is not the case; people merely follow its name in vain.
How deeply one disregards the Way! When Emperor Ming of the Tang dynasty reached Shu, he discussed dozens of men with Pei Shiyan, and there was not one who did not prove worthy.
Yet when it came to Li Linfu, he remarked, "This man is envious of the virtuous and jealous of the capable; he promotes no one his equal.
From this, we know that Emperor Ming knew Linfu was unfit for office, yet he employed him. He knew he was unfit, yet he employed him.
This was because Emperor Ming possessed a mind that held the world in low esteem. When Emperor Dezong discussed Lu Ji with Lu Zhi, he said:
"The whole world knows that Ji is a traitor, yet I alone do not know it. Why is this? Now, the reason Emperor Dezong did not recognize Ji’s treachery was that he held the Dao in low esteem.
Had he truly known how to revere the Dao, he would have surely turned inward and sought [the truth within himself].
This is the principle of the world. When the principles of the world are attained, how could the wicked and depraved ever be able to obscure them?
That Emperor Ming treated the world with contempt and Emperor Dezong treated the Way with contempt both resulted in great thieves bringing chaos to the world.
Likewise, those who practice meditation are unable to use the power of wisdom to destroy ignorance; they reach old age and death without having found the leisure to do so—how tragic!
Now, the Lotus Sūtra says: "You must not take pleasure in dwelling within the burning house of the triple world.
Do not crave coarse, inferior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. If you become attached through craving, you will be consumed by fire."

The tradition records: Udraka Rāmaputra, by means of mundane wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), suppressed the afflictions of the lower stages, attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
At that time, the ruler of the land held him in high esteem and welcomed him into the inner palace; the women there prostrated themselves at his feet.
When Udraka Rāmaputra touched the hand of a woman, he immediately gave rise to sensual desire and consequently lost his supernormal powers. Having finished his meal, he walked away slowly.
He returned to the mountains. Thus, a verse says: "As soon as a single thought of desire arises, one immediately loses the five supernormal powers.

The *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhi-citta-śūramgama-sūtra* (Complete Enlightenment Sutra) states: "It is like the light of the eyes that clearly perceives objects before it; that light is perfectly full and complete, free from both aversion and attachment."
The Transmission says: "The sixth consciousness is characterized by discrimination when active; when inactive, it is equal to and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.

The five types of direct-perception consciousnesses (*pratyakṣa*) likewise—each and every sense faculty is entirely pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. When the eye sees form, that form cannot be apprehended; from the beginning, it is equal to the Dharma-realm.
The same applies to each of the ears, nose, tongue, and body. The direct perception of the five consciousnesses is called..."
Regarding "perfected" (*pariniṣpanna*): Yongming said, "At first, it abides within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of perfected reality, before the floating dust of sensory objects has arisen;
later, it falls into the realm of the cognitive faculty (*manas*), where external forms have withdrawn their shapes. It is for this reason [that it is so called]."
A verse from the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: "As long as there is anything established, all is delusion;
if one perceives only the single mind, then there is no dispute."
The *Chuan* (Biographies) records that Han Yu asked Master Dadian, "How many years of life do you have?

Dadian held up his rosary and showed it to him, saying, "One hundred and eight, day and night. Han Yu was left bewildered. He then asked the First Seat, "The old monk said 'one hundred and eight, day and night';
what is the meaning of this? The First Seat merely clicked his teeth together. On another day...
He then saw Dadian. He asked, "What is the meaning of the 'one hundred and eight' [recitations] performed day and night?
Dadian also clicked his teeth. Thereupon, Taisu withdrew and said with joy, "Now I know that the Buddha-dharma has no dual paths.
He once asked the Head Seat, and the Head Seat’s response was likewise the same. Thereafter, Dadian summoned the First Seat and questioned him; he too confirmed it.
However, Dadian chased him away with his staff. Fengyang’s verse says: "Understanding and deploying the sharp edge of the spiritual faculty is Dadian;
It is clearly known that this is no small matter. The same clacking of teeth, yet the monastic community differs; Only after leaving the monastery did Han Gong find leisure."
Yongming said: "When Layman Pang asked Mazu, 'If water has no sinews or bones, how can it support a ten-thousand-hu boat?
Mazu replied, 'In this place of mine, there is neither water nor boat; what sinews or bones are you looking for? When Deshan arrived at Longtan, he had long heard of Longtan;
yet when he actually arrived, the pond was not to be seen and the dragon did not appear. Deshan replied:"
The Master went in person to Longtan. Minister Chen asked Dongshan, "Among the fifty-two stages of the Bodhisattvas, why is the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (Miaojue) not seen?
He replied, "Minister, you have personally seen Wondrous Enlightenment."
The *Chunqiu* states: During the Eastern Han, Zhang Feng, the Governor of Zhuo Commandery, raised troops in rebellion and styled himself the Unsurpassed General (*Wushang Jiangjun*).
For four years he joined forces with Peng Chong. Ji Zun, together with Zhu You, Geng Yan, and Liu Xi, jointly attacked him.
Zun’s troops arrived first and launched an urgent assault on Feng. Meng Hong, the Clerk of Works for Feng, seized him and surrendered. Previously, Feng had been fond of occult arts;
a Daoist practitioner had told him he was destined to be the Son of Heaven, and had tied a stone wrapped in a five-colored pouch to Feng’s elbow.
He said, "There is a jade seal within this rock. Feng believed him and subsequently rebelled. Once captured and facing execution, he still claimed, "There is a jade seal in my elbow-stone.
Sun Zun struck it with a mallet and shattered it; Feng was struck dumb with astonishment as he met his death. Xi Yin of the Jin dynasty remained loyal to the royal house.
His son, Chao, enjoyed great renown and was a partisan of Huan Wen. Yin detested Wen but was unaware that his son was on friendly terms with him.
As Chao was about to die, he entrusted a chest of books to a disciple, saying, "I originally intended to burn these;

however, I fear that my father’s advanced age might cause him distress and illness upon hearing of this. After my death, if he suffers a decline in his sleep or appetite, you may present this chest to him."
Later, Xi (郗愔) indeed felt grief and lamentation. His disciples presented this to him, and they all exchanged secret plans with Wen (王溫).
Xi was greatly incensed and said, "That young fellow died too late; I shall not weep for him again. Zhang Feng (張豐) was struck with astonishment by this. Xi did not weep.
Together with Pang Gong (龐公), they went to Jiangxi (江西). Deshan (德山) saw Longtan (龍潭). This was Master Chen (陳公).
Upon arriving at Dongshan, the seasonal conditions were exactly the same.
In the Linji school, there are four phrases concerning guest and host: the guest within the guest, the host within the guest, the guest within the host, and the host within the host.
The *Chuan* (Biographies) states: When Chan Master Dongshan Liangjie was first traveling to seek teachers, he journeyed together with his senior companion, Master Mi.

As they passed beneath Longshan (present-day Lingshan) in Changsha, they saw vegetable leaves floating down the mountain stream. Liangjie turned back to gaze at the peaks and ridges, which were profoundly majestic and beautiful.
He said to Mimi, "There must certainly be a recluse here. They then proceeded along the stream for about ten *li*.
There was an old monk with a massive goiter who, placing his hand upon his forehead, called out, "There is no path here; how have you all come by yourselves?"
Jia said, "Setting aside for a moment the fact that there is no path, from where did you enter, Master of the Hermitage? He replied, "I have never been a wandering monk.
Jia said, "How long has the Master lived on this mountain? He replied, "I do not involve myself with spring or autumn.
Jia said, "Did you live here first, or did this mountain exist first? He replied, "I do not know. Jia said, "Why do you not know? He replied, "I do not..."
Once, a person from among humans and devas came. Jia asked, "What principle have you realized that you have come to dwell on this mountain?
He replied, "I saw two clay oxen fighting and entering the sea; even until now, there has been no news. Jia then stepped down from his seat and bowed to him.
He asked, "What is the guest within the host? [The monk] said, "Green mountains shroud white clouds. He asked again, "What is..."
The Master of Masters said, "For many years I have not stepped outside my door. He asked again, "How far apart are guest and host? He replied, "Waves upon the waters of the Long River.
He asked again, "When guest and host meet, what words are spoken? He replied, "A clear breeze brushes against the white moon. Jia bowed once more.
The old monk looked at him with a smile and spoke this verse: "Three bays of thatch-roofed hut from long ago..."
Abiding in the Way, a single ray of divine light leaves the myriad realms at peace. Do not come with judgments of right and wrong to debate me;
the artificial constructions of this floating life have no connection [to the Truth]. Thereupon, he burned his own hut and entered deep into the layered peaks.
Guanjia said, "This old man met the Great Master Mazu of Jiangxi, yet the transmission of his name was lost. While residing at Xinfeng Cave, Guanjia asked a monk with composure: "What..."

"This is your true master. He replied, "The one currently responding to me. The Master looked up at him and sighed in lamentation, saying, "This is what is called 'the horse behind and the donkey in front.
How can you mistake this for your own self? The Buddha-dharma is sinking into oblivion."
"This is merely a preliminary sign. You have not yet clarified the 'host within the guest,' let alone the 'host within the host. The monk asked, 'What is the host within the host?
Jia said, 'Try saying it yourself. The monk replied, 'If one could say it, one would still only be the host within the guest.'"

[The student] asked, "I do not yet understand what it means to be the 'Master among Masters. Yunju Jia remained silent for a long while and then said, "I shall not decline to speak for you, but it is also very difficult to maintain continuity.
In my view, the intention of this old monk of Longshan was like Xiao He’s recognition of Han Xin;
how could there be any fixed dharma? Furthermore, when compared to the words of Dongshan Jia, they are like Huo Guang’s conduct at court—every movement and pause is deliberate and purposeful.
There are also rules and measures for this. Alas! It is certain that later generations will not see the complete works of the ancients.
I, Jia, also regard the "Master among Masters" as something startling and strange; it is indeed questionable.
The Yunmen school has three phrases, namely: "The sky contains the lid," "The eye matches the scale," and "Not entangled in worldly conditions.

The tradition says: When Chan Master Yunmen Wenyan first heard that there was a master named Chenshusu (Venerable Chen) at the Old Temple in Muzhou, who had studied under Huangbo Xiyun, he went to visit him.
Just as he was about to knock on the door, the Venerable Chen suddenly appeared.
As [Yunmen] was leaving, [Xuedou] grabbed him and said, "Speak! Speak! Yunmen was startled and did not know how to answer.
Thereupon, Xuedou pushed him away, saying, "A cartwheel from the Qin dynasty," and immediately shut the door. Yunmen broke a leg and attained realization of the essential meaning beneath these words.
Since he already had a community of followers, he used these three phrases as a teaching; this is an explanation of the phrase, "A cartwheel from the Qin dynasty."
The Lotus Sūtra states: "He has attained the samādhi of the languages of all sentient beings. And the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states:
"He skillfully enters the dhāraṇī of sounds. It is for this reason.
Chou Guo said, "Guo Jian, eh!
Whenever Yunmen was walking about and encountered a monk, he would invariably look at him specifically and say, "Jian. If the monk wished to respond, he would say, "Eh!"
This was taken as their constant practice. Thus, the *Record of the Disciples* (Mén-dí-zǐ-lù) states: "Gù Jiàn Yí" (Gu Jieyi).
Chan Master Yuánmíng Mì deleted the character "Gù," using only the two characters "Jiàn Yí" as a verse; this was called the "Extraction of Gu Verse" (Chōu-gù-sòng).
Now, his descendants have lost its essential meaning; when meeting others, they stare with angry eyes, claiming this is "stimulating" (tísī) and calling it "not failing to recognize."
Regarding "sound and form," it is said that one should offer an answer immediately upon being questioned; this has been handed down as the "eye of the Way.
Master Zu of Beita laughed at this alone and composed a verse, saying: "Yunmen draws back his gaze and laughs with delight; If you hesitate, you will meet his 'gaze and the sound of 'ei' (a shout).
Even if Zhang Li were full of cleverness and skill, In the end, he would find no way to apply it here."
Daowu and Shishuang were father and son. There are those of royal lineage and those of ministerial lineage;

there is the inner succession and the outer succession. The Transmission says: "In the Tang dynasty, both Guo Zhongling and Li Xiping were called 'Wang' (Kings), yet they did not possess [royal] lineage;
they attained that status through their meritorious services. As for the Prince of Qin under the High Ancestor and Suzong under Emperor Ming, they were so because they were born as emperors."
Every family has its own lineage; these are not attained through meritorious service. What is called "internal succession" is a merit achieved without effort;
the former sages valued this. What is called "external succession" is so because it borrows from the achievements of others.
Therefore, it is also called "Borrowing Phrases. Chan Master Caoshan Chang said: "The essence of wondrous clarity fully knows how to avoid injury and offense;
its power lies in encountering conditions without borrowing from them. Chan Master Yunju Hongjue said:

"Penetrating every point and communicating through every thing, such a person is merely called one who has 'accomplished the task,' but is never called 'noble. From this, one should know what is truly noble."
They parted ways from that point on.
Chan Master Deshan Xuanjian said: "When there are words, one rides the tiger's head and gathers its tail; under the first phrase, the fundamental principle is clarified.
When there are no words, the sharp edge of the spiritual mechanism is exposed directly, like a flash of lightning or a stroke of a whisk."

The *Chuan* says: Master Yantou Quanhuo said, "Simply clarify the fundamental principle (*gangzong*); fundamentally there is no substantial dharma. Have you not heard it said that 'it is neither real nor false'?
If you look toward the matter above, you will see it quickly; if you search within the root of the intellect, you will ultimately fail to grasp it.
He further said, "This is the livelihood of those who transcend the ordinary; it merely reveals a tiny fragment right before one's eyes."
It is like an electric brush; it is like sparks struck from flint. Cut off both ends, and you will be spiritually alert and free.
If you say there is a dharma or a matter above this, you are being deceived by the sound of a real bowl;

you are being deluded and bound by it. The ancients called this the "donkey tethering stake. If one were to give actual reality to others, even earth could not contain it. Now, as for what is called "cutting off":
Regarding "cutting off both ends," Kāśyapa smiled; it was neither speech nor silence. Thus, Fenyang’s verse says: "Venerable Kāśyapa, together realizing the illumination;
a blink of the eye, respectfully executing the True Command. This is like the analogy of a flash of lightning or sparks struck from flint.
I have once composed a verse on this: "To give people the actual Dharma is difficult for them to digest; the Way..."
When has fire ever burned one’s mouth? It casts out the carriage-rimmed drill of the Qin era; its protruding peak is like a sheng-measure, swaying at both ends.
The character "Mi" (rice) inscribed at the beginning of the scripture—
The biography states: Formerly, when I arrived in Linchuan, I became close friends with Zhu Xianmu Shiying. Shortly thereafter, the Elder of Shanglan in Nanchang arrived.
Shanglan was naturally distinguished and refined; he said to Shiying, "Juefan is known only for his skill in poetry.
As for Chan, even his master errs, so how much more so his disciples? Shiying laughed and said, "If the Master can..."

"Shall we test this? Shanglan replied, "Yes. After a day had passed, while traveling together to Shushan and dining at an inn, Shanglan said to me, "On the covers of the sutra scrolls, there must be a title with this character [米-木+八]; what is its meaning?
I drew a circle with my finger and ran a horizontal line through it, saying, "This is its meaning. Shanglan was struck dumb with astonishment. I then—
He spoke a verse, saying: "Because it is not formed by letters, it is not the eight [consciousnesses]. The Dharmakāya sleeps soundly, with nothing to block or confine.
When a patch-robed monk faces it, he does not know its name; before a hundred people, it cannot be called forth. Thereupon, Shanglan was displeased.
Upon returning, he recounted this to Shiying. Shiying clapped his hands and said, "Who would have thought that even a 'poetry-monk' understands the meaning of characters?
Now both men have become figures of a thousand ages; reflecting on this in retrospect, one cannot help but feel profound sorrow.
I have heard that Fenyang once composed a verse on a yellow calf, which says: "To have a head but no horns is truly lamentable; through a hundred kalpas, one cannot escape this."

This is a verse by the Master; neither ordinary people nor sages can fully comprehend it. There are some aspects of its manifest appearance that may be grasped, yet I consider this verse to be an interpretation of the meanings and definitions of other characters as well.
If the souls in the Nine Original Plains could be brought back to life, there would surely be one among the world’s eminent scholars who would clap his hands in laughter.
Linji said, "In general, when expounding the Dharma of our school, one must have the Three Mysteries within a single phrase, and the Three Essentials within each Mystery.
Thus, there must be both Mysteries and Essentials."
The Transmission says: "In the past, while I was dwelling in a hermitage beneath Mount Jiufeng in Gaoyang, a monk asked me:
'In the assembly of Linji, two monks once met and simultaneously let out a shout. Upon hearing this, Linji ascended the seat and said:'"
"Great assembly, you must understand Linji’s phrase on guest and host. Go and ask the two Chan practitioners in the hall.
A monk then asked, "Which one is the guest? Which one is the host? Linji said, "Guest and host are clearly distinct.

Just as I was about to offer a reply, I suddenly realized the essential meaning of the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials. Thereupon, I prostrated twice and said, "How great! Unconditioned stillness..."
It is the banner that extinguishes [delusion]. Even if one were to hear of it throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, the thieving mind would perish entirely;
how much more so for me, who lived some two hundred years after the Great Master? Thus, I composed this verse: Within a single phrase, the three mysteries are complete;
Within a single mystery, the three essentials are contained. To examine them closely is to fall into the tiger’s trap; Suddenly, with a single thunderous roar, the drum of lethal poison sounds.
The thieving mind is utterly extinguished; the eyes are dazed and bewildered. The hair stands on end like bristles in the dream of a barren woman.
Chan Master Mingzhao Qian’s verse says: "The lion teaches its cub the methods of delusion; It leaps forward and suddenly turns its body around.
In the place where patterns are woven and horns interlace, The hawk-eye and dragon-pupil lose their true sight."
The *Biographies* state: Four generations after Deshan came Xiqian. Xiqian was short of stature yet possessed sharp, brilliant faculties; the monastic communities called him "The One-Eyed Dragon.
While traveling to visit various teachers, he was still young, yet the elders all feared and were awestruck by him.

Once, while warming himself by a brazier with a monk, the monk asked: "An ancient said, 'Before one's eyes there is no dharma; the meaning lies before one's eyes. It is not a dharma of the present moment, nor..."
Within these four phrases that reach the ears and eyes, which phrase is the guest and which is the host?
Xuefeng Qian pointed to the fire and said, "Can you pluck out a single eyebrow from within this for me?
The monk replied, "Not only would I lose my life, but all the people in the entire world would do so. Qian said, "Why do you grasp it yourself?"
Ji Touxia was about to pass away. As he ascended the seat, he said: "In a hundred years, one looks only for today;
what of the affairs of today? I have dwelt on this mountain for forty years, using only a single sword to bring life to the eyes of men.
He then picked up his headcloth and said: "Is there now anyone like Cunda? Holding it up for all directions to behold, he unfurled it and cast it down.
Shi. A monk asked, "When Cunda makes his final offering with such earnest devotion, what is it like? Qian said, "Do not let us be at fault.
The monk asked again, "When the Master passes away, where will you go? Qian lifted his foot and said, "Look beneath your feet."
He asked again, "A hundred years from now, what will serve as the ultimate standard? Qian threw his handkerchief down.
The monks bowed twice and withdrew to their places. Thereupon, Qian spoke a verse: "Brandishing full majesty within the belly of a sword— You people, all of you, must guard it well.
An iron ox gives birth to a calf amidst the flames; Who at this parting can grasp my intent? Having finished speaking, he passed away.
And thus he was transformed.
The *Sutra of Forty-two Sections* says: "One must resign one's life when facing the difficulty of death.
The *Biographies* state: When Han Xin was the Marquis of Huaiyin, he feigned illness and did not attend court, while Chen Xi served as Chancellor for a generation. He passed by...
Xi Xin took him by the hand and walked with him around the courtyard several times. Looking up at the sky, he sighed and said, "Can you engage in discourse with me?
I wish to have words with you. Xi Xin replied, "It is as the General commands.
Xi Xin said, "The place where you reside is where the world's finest troops are stationed. Furthermore, you are a trusted and favored minister of His Majesty. People—"
He said, "If you go back once, Your Majesty will not believe you; if you go a second time, he will become suspicious; if you go a third time, he will surely be enraged and lead the army himself.
I shall rise up from within for you, and the empire can be settled. Xiang Xi replied, "I respectfully accept your instructions. In the tenth year of the Han, Xi indeed rebelled.
Emperor Gao went there in person to lead the campaign, but Xiao He was ill and did not go; instead, he secretly sent men to Xi’s location. And...
He plotted with his subordinates; at night, he falsely proclaimed an amnesty for the various prisoners and slaves, intending to launch a surprise attack on Empress Dowager Gao and the Crown Prince.
Once the deployment was finalized, he awaited the report from Dou Xī. Suddenly, someone informed Empress Dowager Lü, who had him executed in the Zhōngshì chamber.
At that time, Xìn had no troops, yet he said, "I shall rise from within for you. This is indeed suspicious.
Thus, although Xin was executed, could his heart truly have died? When Ma Su was defeated at Jieting, Zhuge Kongming put him to death.
On his deathbed, Ma Su wrote a letter to Kongming, saying: "Your Excellency regards me as a son, and I regard Your Excellency as a father.
I pray you will deeply reflect upon the principle of punishing Gun but exalting Yu, so that our lifelong friendship shall not [be severed]."
If one is deficient in this regard, then even though Xu dies, he will have no regrets in the yellow earth.
At that time, a multitude of one hundred thousand people shed tears for him. Observing this, I believe that the death of Xin was not a true death.
It may be said that Xu’s casting aside of his life was not a true death; is this not so?
The *Yi* (Book of Changes), in the hexagram *Shihe* (Jaw-biting), says: "It is advantageous to administer legal proceedings;
there will be success. The *Commentary* says: "In the past, Chan Master Huanglong Nan resided at Guizong Temple on Mount Lu. One night, it was consumed by fire."
He remained in prison for sixty days without food. Once he was released, he resided at the Southern Pagoda of Shimen. He once said to his disciples:
"While I was in prison, I realized the Bodhisattva’s *līlā-vikrīḍita-samādhi* (Samādhi of the Bodhisattva’s Playful Sport) as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The Sūtra says:"

The Bodhisattva’s playful mastery of supernatural powers and his purification of Buddha-fields are not undertaken out of personal preference, but rather as a rebuke of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), for the latter is incapable of bringing sentient beings to maturity.
A disciple requested to hear his explanation, to which Huanglong replied:

"Whenever a prison official governs those who have committed crimes, he scrutinizes their true intentions and deceptions; once he has identified them, he invariably inflicts severe flogging upon such fraudulent individuals."
When reality is fully exhausted, one is naturally liberated; even if there were cruel punishments, they could not be applied.
Even when the penalty reaches death, one accepts it with a willing heart, for wisdom has ultimately withered the passions.

Now, as for those who study Chan, their madness of frantic seeking and the disease of their deceit cannot be refined away unless tempered by the wisdom of insight (*jñāna*). How, then, can they be liberated? Therefore, throughout their lives, they merely...
I have tested the monastics of the world using three kinds of speech. When I was young, I heard an elder discuss this during a night conversation;
it has now been twenty years. As these teachings are beneficial to the monastic community, I have recorded them here.
Chan Master Xiangyan Xian’s verse says: There is a phrase that is perfectly complete in its measure; If you attempt to deliberate upon it, it carries with it a companion.
If you fail to tread upon it, reflect on its source; Then the lifelong work of study will remain unaccomplished. With earnest diligence, one embraces a sandalwood tree.
The *Biàn* (Tradition) says: The *Zǎobó lùn* (Treatise by Zao Bo) states: "Regarding 'Uragasāra-candana': *uraga* is the name for a snake; *candana* is a fragrant tree.
This clarifies that this snake is most venomous and constantly suffers from the heat of its own poison. By coiling its body around this fragrant tree, its toxic vapors are immediately stilled.
This illustrates that if there are sentient beings who hear it said that both mind and objects are empty and fundamentally non-existent..."
As for its essential nature and characteristics, it has no location and not a single dharma can be apprehended as its fragrance.
By believing and entering into this realization, all the poisonous vapors of affliction are naturally purified.
Thus I know that the saying, "Earnestly embracing and obtaining a sandalwood tree," was not uttered in vain.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "One should not grasp at or adhere to what is said according to conventional expression, for that which is real is free from names and words.
Mahāmati, it is like using a finger to point at an object for a fool; the fool gazes only at the finger and does not perceive the actual object.

In this same way, fools grasp at and adhere to the finger of conventional expression, never letting go until the end, and thus they are ultimately unable to attain that which transcends verbal expression."
This refers to the primary ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
A tradition relates that a monk asked Chan Master Jiufeng: "Is there still Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains? He replied, "There is.
The monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains? He replied, "The large rocks are large; the small rocks are small."
The inferior are inferior. Now, when students hear such statements being raised, they immediately rejoice, believing they have attained understanding.

When questioned further, they say, "Everything one encounters is the absolute reality; it is manifest in every instance. Alas! This is what is meant by "looking at the finger and failing to grasp the actual meaning.
Once, I traveled with a monk from Mount Xiaoyao, passing through a ravine of jagged rocks and entering the Five Peaks.
Resting in the shade of a tree, he recounted this causal occasion and composed a verse, saying: "If the stone head were the Buddha-dharma, The Dharmakāya would not be numinous and holy.
If the Buddha-dharma had great and small, The Dharmakāya would be divided into portions. Upon a withered skull there is no sap;
Even when the patch-robed monk sees it with his own eyes, he does not believe. Of the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates, One phrase is for you."
This concludes the explanation.
*Stonehead’s Capping Verse on the Accordance of Penetration* states: "The nature of the four elements returns of itself, like a child finding its mother.
The Commentary says: "The subtlety of these words is rarely recognized by students. For when a child finds its mother," [it is as if]...
One who does not rely on others for understanding but possesses self-confidence.
When Master Guifeng Zongmi first read the *Nirvana Sutra* (or *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*), he reached the passage: "I now have this body, a combination of the four great elements.
That which is called hair, fur, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, filth, and color—all return to earth. Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, and fluids..."
Saliva, foam, phlegm, tears, vital essence, and the large and small excretions all return to water; warmth returns to fire; movement and transformation return to wind.
When the four great elements have each separated, where then does this illusory body reside? Thereupon, he attained a sudden and profound awakening.
It is like a child finding its mother.
The *Poxinlun* (Treatise on Destroying Form and Mind) states: "That unity is not visible; multiplicity is also not visible; their combination is not visible."
Therefore, there are no external objects (*dharma*). What is the meaning clarified by this verse? You previously stated that the various bases (*āyatana*), such as form and so forth, all truly exist.
Why? Because consciousness is able to apprehend external objects. This argument is not tenable. Why?
There are three reasons why there are no formless entrances (*ārūpyāyatana*). What are these three?

First, it is because [some] falsely imagine that a single atom exists as a substantial reality, like those non-Buddhist followers of the Vaiśeṣika school and others, who conceptually construct [atoms] as existing apart from the head, eyes, limbs, and other parts of the body.
If there truly exists a self (ātman), and likewise subtle atoms (paramāṇu), do they exist as substantial entities apart from color, fragrance, and so forth?
Second, can the distinctions between many real atoms be perceived? Third, can their aggregation as many atoms be perceived?
What is the meaning of this? If those individual atoms were substantially existent, they would be imperceptible, just like that [self].

The non-Buddhist Vaiśeṣikas and others engage in false conceptualization, claiming that apart from the head, eyes, limbs, and other parts of the body, a separate divine self (*ātman*) exists, yet such a thing cannot be perceived.
The same applies to atoms (*paramāṇu*): apart from color, fragrance, and so forth, they cannot be perceived.
Therefore, no single real atom can be seen. Thus, the verse says: "That unity is not visible. If there were truly many [atoms], [the following would apply].
Regarding the differentiation of atoms: if they were distinct, each individual atom should be clearly visible; yet they are not seen.
For this reason, the differentiation of many atoms is likewise invisible. Therefore, the verse says: "Even as a plurality, they are not seen."
As for the claim that a collection of many atoms is invisible, this is also not the case. Why? Because a single atom has no substantial reality;
how, then, could they be combined? Therefore, it is not established. Thus, the verse says: "The combination is invisible.
This is because there is no such thing as an atom. Question: How is it not established? Answer: The verse says: "The six objects are the same..."
At that time, they conjoin. If the atom has six sides, and if these six occupy only one location, then all the great elements would be a single atom. What does this verse clarify?
If atoms come from the six directions and six atoms conjoin, then if this were the case, the atom would have six sides.
If it has six sides, then it possesses six distinct parts. Furthermore, if the atom occupies a specific location, there would be no room [for others].
Regarding the remaining atoms: therefore, the verse says, "The six objects arise simultaneously," because the objects possess six aspects.
If the six subtle atoms were to occupy a single location, then there would be six atoms within the space of one atom. If such were their nature, the six objects would occupy a single place.
If they occupied a single place, then the six objects could not be perceived. Why? Because [the spatial positions] of these and those atoms...
Because there is no distinction. If this were the case, then all coarse objects such as mountains and rivers would likewise be invisible.
Therefore it is said: "If the six [elements] were located in a single place, the great elements would constitute a single atom.
As for a single atom, it is a non-entity, as was answered previously; because the combination of one and many cannot be perceived.
The *Śāstra* says: The Vaiśeṣikas and others give rise to a certain dogmatic adherence, maintaining that apart from the head, eyes, body parts, and so forth, there exists a self (*ātman*).
This self exists but is invisible; therefore, the treatise refers to it as "a single atom" (*paramāṇu*).
If this single atom existed apart from external objects such as form, sound, fragrance, and taste, it would have to exist in the same manner as the self.
It cannot be seen. If the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) truly possessed the characteristics of the six directions, they would be clearly discernible and could not be intermingled;

thus it is said that no other dust can be admitted. Furthermore, if the six objects were inseparable from their combination and thus invisible, then mountains, rivers, and the great earth would likewise be invisible, as they too are all combinations. Within the combination of these objects, [the individual elements] do not...
It can be seen that even in the case of mountains, rivers, and the great earth, they exist through combination; how could they be seen as solitary entities? There is no such principle.

However, the realm of the Buddhas is dense and subtle, difficult to perceive, and cannot be illustrated by worldly analogies. Furthermore, among the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the "cognition of the holy ones' determination" (*ārya-pratyakṣa*).

This refers to those phenomena that do not fall within the scope of ordinary direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or semblance-perception (*ābhāsa*); these are then apprehended by the cognition of the holy ones' determination.
This is established. As the World-Honored One said, "The three realms are mind-only.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Question: How does one hear? Is it heard by means of the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*), by means of the ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*), or by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?
If it were heard by the ear-faculty, it would be untenable, because the ear-faculty lacks the capacity for cognition and awareness.
[Objection: Is it the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) that hears? Since the ear-consciousness lasts for only a single moment, it cannot perform discrimination;

therefore, it should not hear. Or is it the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) that hears? The mental consciousness also cannot hear. Why? Because the five consciousnesses first cognize the five objects, and only then does the mental consciousness cognize them.
The mental consciousness cannot cognize present objects; it cognizes only past and future objects. If [it were] the mind...
If consciousness were able to cognize the five sensory objects of the present, then blind and deaf people should also be able to cognize sounds and forms.

Why? Because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is not impaired. The answer is: It is not the ear-faculty (śrotra-indriya) that hears sound, nor is it the ear-consciousness (śrotra-vijñāna), nor even the mental consciousness.
This matter of hearing sound arises from the conjunction of many causes and conditions; therefore, one is able to hear sound. One cannot say that a single dharma is able to hear.
Sound. Why is this? Because the ear-faculty lacks sentience, it cannot hear sound. Because consciousness is formless, non-obstructive, and locationless, it also does not hear sound.
Since sound lacks sentience and lacks a faculty, it does not know sound. At that time, the ear-faculty is unimpaired.
When sound reaches a place where it can be heard, and the mind has the intention to hear, the sense-object and the mind come into conjunction; thus, ear-consciousness arises accordingly.
From that ear-consciousness, mental consciousness arises, which is able to discern various causes and conditions so as to hear the sound. For this reason, one should not raise the objection:
"Even though sound is heard, in the Buddha-dharma there is no dharma that can act, see, or know. As the verse says:
There is karma and there is its fruit. That there is no fruit for unperformed karma—this is the foremost profundity, which can be seen through the Buddha-dharma.
Though empty, it is not annihilated; though continuous, it is not eternal; and yet neither demerit nor merit is lost. Thus is the Buddha-dharma taught.

The *Chuan* (Biographies) records that a monk once asked Chan Master Heze Shenhui: "When seeing and hearing illuminate sound and form, is there merely simultaneous action, or is there a sequence of before and after?
He replied: "Let us set aside for now the questions of simultaneous action and sequence;
ultimately, what do you take to be sound and form? The monk said: "According to what the Master has discussed, then no sound or form can be apprehended."
Thereupon, he prostrated twice and departed that very day. Later, he lived in seclusion on Mount Meng.
When the Chan Master Nian of Mount Shou was asked by a monk, "What is the Buddha? he replied, "The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while the mother-in-law leads it.
The monk asked, "I do not understand the meaning of this. He replied, "A centenarian has lost his father. The monk said, [I do not understand].
"A hundred-year-old man—how could he have a father? Shoushan said, "You understand. He further said, "This is sitting alone, where there is neither superior nor inferior;
from the beginning, not a single dharma has been given to anyone."
The Transmission says: At Mount Shou, there was the eminent disciple, Chan Master Shen Dingyin. He once asked a monk to explain this saying, and composed a verse:
“The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it; Who is behind, and who is ahead? If someone asks again, one must reply:
The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it. This old man [Dingyin] relied upon teacherless wisdom (*asatkalpa-jñāna*) and spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*).

He uttered words that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), capable of describing that wondrousness which cannot be transmitted. An elderly man dwelt in the mountains, and students followed him.
When someone asked a question and he remained silent, they suspected that he was unwilling to speak for their sake.

When he did answer questions, it was by using words to dispel words—a matter of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). This intention has a long history. Once, Ānanda...
Kāśyapa asked, "World-Honored One, besides entrusting you with the golden robe, what further Dharma did he transmit? Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda!
Ānanda responded. Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate."
Master Baogong’s Verses on the Twelve Hours say: At the hour of eating: Ignorance is fundamentally the body of Śākyamuni. Sitting or lying down, one does not know that the source is the Way;
thus one merely hurries about in vain, undergoing bitter toil. Recognizing sounds and forms, seeking out the distant and the near—this is nothing but a person defiled by the past.
If you wish to seek the Buddha-way with the mind, ask the void and only then will you emerge from the dust.
The Transmission says: A monk asked Yun’an, “What is the Way? Yun’an said, “Master Bao said:
‘If you wish to seek the Buddha-way with the mind, ask empty space; only then will you leave the dust behind. Now that you seek the Buddha-way, what does empty space say to you?
At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Formerly, Master Liang visited Master Ma.
The Patriarch asked, "You claim to lecture on the sutras; with what do you lecture? He replied, "I lecture with my mind.
The Patriarch said, "The mind is like a skilled performer, and the intellect is like the conductor. How can you lecture on the sutras [with such things]?
Huiliang spoke sharply, saying, "If the mind cannot lecture, could it be that empty space lectures? The Patriarch said, "Indeed, it is empty space that lectures."
Sengliang also attained realization. Returning home, he said to his disciples, "I used to think that in my entire life of lecturing on the teachings, none in the world could surpass me.
Today, upon meeting the venerable elder Daokai, it was all wiped away in a single spittle. My previous understanding was entirely deceiving you.
He then crossed the Zhang River and lived in seclusion in the Western Mountains. I once composed a *Yufu ci* (Fisherman’s Song) concerning this.
He sang of his own character and style, saying: "In the lecture hall, heavenly flowers follow the jade whisk; In the heart of the waves, where can the moon be grasped?
The old masters in the neighboring houses steal my annotations; Turning my head to look, the void suddenly speaks on its own.
Returning to face my disciples, I recount it once more: My former understandings have all deceived you; Beyond the shore lies a mountain shrouded in evening rain."
Suddenly he departed; amidst a thousand crags and ten thousand ravines, there was no place to be found.
Regarding the noble and precious instructions of Dongshan, the transmission says:
Master Yunju Deng said, "When members of the Sangha speak or breathe, there must be a source for it; do not..."

Do not treat this as something trivial. What kind of place is this? How can you accept it so easily? Whenever you ask about a matter, you must recognize at least a little of what is good and what is bad.

If you do not distinguish between the honorable and the humble, the noble and the lowly, and fail to understand what constitutes an offense, then speaking recklessly and at random will be of no benefit.
You all travel together on foot, seeking out similar words everywhere; therefore—
I usually tell my brothers: "Do not take offense at our lack of resemblance; I fear that too many fellow students will depart. Above all, do not bring them here.
If they are brought here, they will not be like us. One must also examine the beginning and end of one's speech.
An eighty-year-old elder entering the examination hall—this is no child’s play. It is no matter of casual indifference. A single word out of alignment..."
"Thousands of miles, ten thousands of miles—it is difficult to bring it under control. This is because the objects of study are too easy. He further said:
"You people here, even if you were to master the matters on the Buddha’s side, you would already have misapplied your minds.
Have you not seen how the ancients could make the heavens rain flowers and the stones nod their heads? Even that did not concern one's own self; as for anything else, what is it?"
Xian: "Now, if you intend to take this finite body and mind and apply it toward the infinite, what connection can there possibly be?
It would be like trying to fit a square block into a round hole; how much friction and discord that would cause!

If such a thing did not exist, even if you could speak with the splendor of clustered flowers and brocade, it would be of no use. You have not yet escaped the realm of consciousness and emotion; all matters must [be resolved accordingly]."
Only when you have exhausted everything here will you be free from fault; only then can you emerge from the body.

If even a single hair’s breadth remains unexhausted, you are immediately entangled by worldly dust; how much more so if it is greater? To err by a hair’s breadth is to commit a transgression as vast as a mountain.
As the ancients said: "The place of study is not profound; it is entirely mundane. One cannot bear to abandon the things of the inner chambers. All together.
This is a leakage. You must simply, right here, engage in taking, engaging in going, and engaging in coming, until all affairs are completely exhausted;
only then will you be free from fault. It is like a person who has mastered every head of business and penetrated every object;
such a one is merely called a "person of affairs," but is never called "noble. Know that the path of the noble is distinct by itself; it is indeed the world.
One must not bring extremely heavy or extremely precious objects before those who are honorable and noble;
one must know that this is inconceivable and should not be treated with ordinary concern. Thus, the ancients said: "It is like two mirrors facing each other;
their radiance reflects one another, and there is neither deficiency nor excess. Is this not simply the same? Yet it is still called a matter of reflections. As it is said:
When the sun rises and illuminates the world, that clarity is one half. What is that other half called?
Nowadays, people have not yet recognized the coarse and shallow matters at the gate of light and shadow; they take these for the affairs of the inner chamber, but how can that suffice?
It is also said: "The matter of ascending to heaven must be proclaimed before the assembly; it is a matter of complete perfection."
He cast it away before the assembly; when thrown to the ground, it made a sound like gold. He did not turn his head back to look at it. What other use could there be for such things?

Did you not see that when the Second Patriarch was young, he had extensively studied poetry and the classics, and understood the Three Baskets of the Holy Teachings as clearly as looking at the palm of his hand?
For what reason, then, did he further seek from Bodhidharma the "settling of the mind"? From this, one should know that the matters within this Gate are not [ordinary].
Trivialities! As I savor Yunju’s words, I know that the meaning of the "Noble and Precious" must be realized through one's own awakening. Alas!
It was Yao and Shun who brought peace to the world simply by wearing their ceremonial robes.

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: Bodhisattva Vajragarbha asked the World-Honored One, "If all sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, for what reason do they still possess all ignorance?
If this ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the beginning, by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further say that they have been Buddhas from the beginning?
That ordinary beings throughout the ten directions have been established in the Buddha-way from the start, yet subsequently give rise to ignorance..."
[Mañjuśrī] asked: "At what time do all Tathāgatas again give rise to all afflictions? The World-Honored One replied:

"Good son, throughout all worlds, from beginning to end, arising and ceasing, prior and subsequent, existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing, starting and stopping—these continuous, successive moments, revolving in cycles, with their various graspings and relinquishings, are all saṃsāra.
Without having escaped saṃsāra, one attempts to discern the Perfect [Nature]."

If one perceives that nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ālayavijñāna*) as being identical to the process of transmigration, there would be no way to escape the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
The *Chuan* (Commentary) states: Guifeng said, "This section exhaustively resolves profound doubts. Therefore, the Bodhisattva’s objection implies:

"If sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, then since they currently possess ignorance (*avidyā*), the Tathāgatas of the ten directions should likewise subsequently become afflicted by defilements. The Buddha replied:

The meaning is this: this very discrimination is itself ignorance; therefore, even upon seeing Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*), one still undergoes the cycle of transmigration, just as when clouds move, the moon appears to move.
However, if for a single moment not a thought arises, then the boundaries of past and future are severed—like cataracts clearing and the [illusory] flowers vanishing.
Sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, yet few are able to know this; those who know have little faith, and those who believe rarely attain understanding. Even if they understand...
It is difficult to reach this realm. "Cuiyan Zhen Dianxiong, you should ask the monk: Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas;
why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi? Wangming came from below; why was he able to emerge from the woman’s samādhi?
When no one could answer, only Ying of Shaowu, at the moment of the question, pinched him with his hand.
He rose from his knees and departed. Zhen laughed and said, "The guest who sells spoons and chopsticks has not yet arrived.
I consider that Ying of Shaowu may indeed be one for whom not a single thought arises and for whom the past and future limits have been severed.

The Chan Master Yongming was once asked by a monk: "Taking the mind as the fundamental principle is the true pulse of the Chan gate. Now, 'mind' is merely a name; what serves as its substance? The Master replied:

"Since recent times, scholars of the present day have for the most part clung to the words while turning their backs on the intent. They are muddled regarding the substance and identify only with the name.

How can those who recognize the name while forgetting the substance ever exhaustively reach the ground of reality? How can those who follow the words while being lost in the intent ever achieve resonance with it?"
The source of the Way is simply the mind; it takes knowing as its substance. This is numinous knowing, whose nature is inherently spiritual and liberated.

It is not like deluded consciousness, which relies on conditions, depends upon objects, and knows through deliberate effort. Nor is it like the vast emptiness of space, which is a state of total annihilation and lack of cognition.
The *Biàn* says: The *Zhàolùn* states that "Prajñā is without cognition" because it is devoid of cognition that grasps at signs.
Ordinary people all claim that Prajñā is wisdom (*jñāna*), and that wisdom entails cognition. If there were cognition, there would be grasping and attachment;
if there were grasping and attachment, one would not accord with non-arising (*anutpāda*). Now, it is clarified that the true wisdom of Prajñā is signless and objectless; although...
One mirrors ultimate truth and does not grasp at signs; therefore, it is said that there is "no-knowing. Thus, a sutra says:
"The holy mind has no knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know. Furthermore, a sutra says: "True prajñā is pure as empty space;

it is without knowing, without seeing, without action, and without conditions. This means that knowing is itself non-knowing; it does not depend on the act of forgetting. It is by this [that one realizes it].
Knowing the truth, this knowing does not fall within the realm of existence or non-existence. For this reason, the Buddhas have their secrets and the teachings of secrecy;

the Patriarchs have their silent transmission and the school of secret entrustment. It can only be realized through personal introspection and resonance; it is not something expressed through the mediation of words.
One who clarifies the essence is clearly aware and unclouded, remaining in a state of tranquil, constant knowing. —Yuanwu of Weifeng.
The Zen Master said: "The Buddha-dharma is present in the midst of daily activities—in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; in drinking tea and eating meals;
in speaking and conversing with one another. Yet it is not found in any actions performed, nor in the raising of the mind or the stirring of a thought."
Regarding Linji’s Four Cries, the Transmission says:
"The Vajra King Sword is manifest and majestic; as soon as it touches the lips, one strikes its edge.
The Earth-Sawing Lion has no fixed nest; to hesitate or wait for a mechanism to act is immediately to incur leakage. The probing pole and shadow-grass..."
"Not entering the monastery boundaries; not a single point arrives. The thief’s own body is defeated.
Sometimes a shout is not used as a shout. The Buddha-dharma is vast; it is simply a toothache. These four verses were composed by me when I was thirty-five years old.
Now, at fifty-two, I happened to read them while looking through my old books. Thereupon, I sighed deeply. Formerly, Li... [text ends]
Bei Hai was renowned in the world for his calligraphy, and people vied with one another to take him as their master of brushwork. Bei Hai laughed and said, "Those who copy me will be clumsy;
those who merely resemble me will die. These four lines of verse have a profound meaning, much like the case of those who study Bei Hai’s calligraphy and end up merely resembling it.
Shoushan ascended the hall and said, "In the past, Master Xinghua addressed the assembly, saying: 'O Great Assembly! Master Xinghua...'"
"I cannot let you all go; you must not ask 'how' or 'what. You must enter directly with a single blade.
Xinghua shall provide testimony for you. At that time, the Elder Minde came forward from the assembly, bowed, and as soon as he rose, he shouted.
Xinghua also shouted. Minde shouted again, and Xinghua shouted again. Minde then ceased. Xinghua then said:
If it had been anyone else who just came here, he would have received thirty blows—not even a single blow less. Why?
Because that Minde knew how to employ a shout not as a mere shout. Shoushan said, "Look at how Xinghua employs it in this way."
"Why did he let him pass? O Senior Elders, tell me: in what sense does the first shout not function as a shout?

A Song of the Way. It describes the six perfections, taking patience as the foremost: "Let others slander me; let others be wrong.

Chan Master Jianlong Qing of Yangzhou possessed exemplary conduct.

Because one is constantly able to practice great relinquishment, it is called the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). Wearing plain clothing and maintaining purity is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
Wearing disheveled hair and marring one’s appearance is called patience (*kṣānti*). When the mind is never in harmony with worldly concerns, it is called diligence (*vīrya*).

Using wisdom and compassion to benefit the mundane world while not dwelling with consciousness is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Having already attained the fruit of Buddhahood, the supramundane sublime wisdom is called... [the perfection of wisdom].

Wisdom is to dwell perpetually within birth and death to guide and receive sentient beings; furthermore, while lacking the karma of a woman, manifesting the reception of a female body clarifies the practice of great compassion—this is called skillful means (*upāya*).
To constantly follow great vows and rescue beings throughout the six realms is called great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*).

To fear neither birth nor death and constantly turn the wheel of Dharma is called power (*bala*). Following wisdom, one manifests through illusion in all oceans of lands, constantly bestowing [benefits].
Buddhist practice is what is called wisdom. To be fully endowed with these ten *pāramitās*, [the Master] said:

A sutra states: "That which can be spoken is called a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*);

Why is this? That which is spoken is called a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, is not [conditioned].
This is conditioned; therefore, there is no speech. Furthermore, there is no speaker, just as an infant’s speech is not yet articulate.
Although such an infant has speech, in reality, they have no speech. The Tathāgata is likewise. That which is not yet articulated is precisely the secret.

This is understood through the analogy of the hexagram *Li*. Just as when one removes the six lines of *Li*, they are interchanged—alternating between the biased and the correct—to form three layers; and when these transformations are exhausted, they become five.

Thus, I have ventured to speak in detail upon matters that former sages strictly forbade, even if it means incurring the offense of my predecessors or receiving slander from those who come after.
Yet I am determined to ensure that you hear this, for within the Buddha-dharma, [this act] is equivalent to saving a pigeon or feeding a tiger.
Within the ways of the world, such was the resolve of Cheng Ying, Gongsun Chujiu, Guangao, and Tian Guang. Alas! How virtuous they were!
This postscript was written by the layman Xu Yi Yanzhou, a *icchantika*, on the final day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Xiangxing era.
